results.quote: An LLM might judge whether the evidence is sufficient, whether a recommendation is well supported, or whether an agent appears to have completed the task. ... Deterministic code can decide what combination of those judgments and other facts is required before the workflow moves forward.
results.reason: The passage, under the point that the pattern applies inside applications, states both halves of the claim: the LLM judges these three things and deterministic code decides the required combination before the workflow proceeds.

results.quote: This sort of combined deterministic / non-deterministic logic is one of the biggest opportunities available at the application layer.
results.reason: The passage states the claim almost word for word.

results.quote: A judge that is slightly noisy in an offline eval may be annoying. ... The same judge sitting in front of every important action can create loops, block good work, approve bad work, and add latency to every execution.
results.reason: The passage makes the same contrast with the same hedges and the same list of harms.

results.quote: the judge is still an LLM. ... It can make mistakes for all the same reasons the model doing the work can. ... One way to handle this is to stop treating a single judge as authoritative.
results.reason: The first two parts are asserted. The passage only offers not treating a single judge as authoritative as 'one way to handle' the problem, while the claim states flatly that a single judge should not be treated as authoritative.

results.quote: It supports model-based graders alongside deterministic graders such as string checks and Python code, and multiple graders can be combined into a larger evaluation.
results.reason: The preceding sentence identifies the subject as OpenAI's grader architecture, and the passage states the claim directly.

results.quote: [MAJ-EVAL](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.790/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), for example, creates multiple evaluator agents representing different dimensions of the evaluation and lets them deliberate over the result.
results.reason: The passage states exactly what the claim says about MAJ-EVAL.

results.quote: An answer can be correct but incomplete. - It can be well written but unsupported by the source material. - Or an agent can arrive at the right result after taking actions it should never have taken.
results.reason: The passage opens by saying much judging boils down to the single question of whether the output was good, then lists the three distinct failures the claim names.

results.quote: For high-volume applications, the economics could matter quite a bit. Because cost is more noticeable when you're running these evals constantly at application runtime, a specialized model that is designed to be cheap for this use case is a good option.
results.reason: The passage says the specialized cheap model is a good option, but hedges that cost 'could' matter, while the claim states flatly that judging cost matters.

results.quote: periodically compare the judge against humans. - If a judgment controls something important, collect examples of those decisions and have people independently evaluate them. - Measure where the judge disagrees, and change the rubric, model, context, or decision boundary when the disagreement is unacceptable.
results.reason: The passage makes the measure-and-change recommendation, but within the condition that the judgment controls something important. The claim drops that condition, so it is broader than the text.

results.quote: Many of the above patterns require that we move LLM judges inside the agent loops and put them in the critical path for our applications
